name: lookup
intent: Resolve a resource's name to its current location - or to the resource itself - through a mediating lookup service, so that clients depend on stable names instead of hard-wired addresses and can re-resolve when the resource moves.
problem: A resource (service, object, file, device, provider implementation) is known by a name, but its location - address, port, URL, file path, bound object or class - is unknown to the client, changes over time, or differs per environment. Hard-wiring the location into every client makes the resource impossible to move, replicate or replace without coordinated redeployment, and leaks environment-specific configuration into application code.
context: Systems whose resources are location-transparent: distributed middleware and naming/directory services, service discovery, plugin and provider architectures, container-managed resources, dynamic linking and device discovery. The pattern applies when names are stable while locations are not, and when a mediating instance that owns the name-to-location bindings - including their registration and invalidation policy - can exist.
benefits: Clients depend on names, not locations: a resource can be moved, replaced or replicated (or resolved differently per environment) without editing client code, because the binding changes in one place.
New resources and providers join by registering a binding, so the client side stays closed for modification (open/closed).
The lookup service is the single place for policy: caching, access control, monitoring, failover and environment selection are applied centrally instead of being re-implemented by every client.
Location transparency lets the same client code work against local, remote or pooled resources and across deployment environments.
Resolution can be cached and amortised: the indirection costs one lookup instead of a re-discovery per use.
Resource users and resource providers are decoupled: providers can appear, disappear or scale out without a client deployment.
tradeoffs: The lookup service is a runtime dependency and a potential single point of failure: when it is unreachable nothing resolves, so it must be replicated, cached or gracefully degraded.

Bindings go stale: a cached name-to-location result is wrong the moment the resource moves; TTL, lease or invalidation policy must be chosen deliberately, and both too-long and too-short lifetimes cause incidents.
Registration and lifecycle become operational work: names, bindings, leases and eviction of dead entries must be managed, audited and bounded.
Indirection hides the concrete target: static analysis, stack traces and reviews no longer show which implementation answers a name, and a misbinding surfaces only at runtime.

The lookup service is a trust boundary: whoever can register or alter bindings can redirect clients to a location of their choosing (spoofing, cache poisoning, rogue providers) unless registration and resolution are authenticated.
Every resolution adds latency and load - negligible for a cached local registry, a real network round trip for a remote naming service.
A successful lookup is not availability: the resolved location can still be down, so clients keep needing timeout, retry and failover handling.

participants.responsibility: Mediating instance that owns the bindings and answers resolution requests; it may cache results, apply policy (access control, selection, failover) and hide the structure of the underlying registry (DNS, naming service, container, provider files).
Stable, location-independent identifier the client uses; it may be flat (a service name) or structured (a compound or path name), and it is the contract between clients and providers.
The thing being located - a service instance, remote object, data source, file, device or provider implementation.
Provider-side role that creates and maintains the binding (register or rebind, renew the lease, deregister) so that resolution reflects reality.
Resource user that resolves a name through the lookup service and treats the result as a binding with a lifetime, not as a constant.

use_cases: Naming and directory services: DNS resolves host names to current addresses; JNDI, CORBA Naming and Jini resolve compound names to bound objects; LDAP/AD resolve names to directory entries.
Service discovery: a client asks for a logical service name and receives a healthy instance address, with instance churn absorbed by leases or health checks that keep the bindings fresh.

Plugin and provider architectures: the application resolves module, extension or provider names to implementations at runtime (ServiceLoader provider files, entry points, dynamic import, plugin.Open), so third parties extend the product without recompiling the client.

Container-managed resources: application code looks up data sources, queues, mail sessions or configuration under deployment names (java:comp/env/..., connection-string names) instead of hard-coded endpoints.
Dynamic linking and loading: importing a library or symbol by name at load time (dlopen/dlsym, Boost.DLL) instead of linking the location statically, so deployments can swap implementations.

Service mesh sidecar: sidecar proxies and ingress gateways resolve logical service names to instance endpoints through the control plane's service registry (e.g., Consul, etcd, Kubernetes API), enabling canary routing, load balancing and failover without client-side service discovery code.

Feature flags and dynamic configuration: a client resolves a feature-flag or config-entry name at runtime from a flag service, allowing toggles, A/B splits and parameter changes to take effect without a redeployment cycle.

Kubernetes Service DNS: a Pod resolves a namespace-qualified Service name instead of an endpoint IP; normal Services resolve to a stable cluster IP while headless Services expose the selected Pod address set for client-side selection.

Consul service discovery: Consul DNS and prepared queries resolve registered service names to healthy instances, with tag or prefix filtering and datacenter failover kept in lookup policy rather than copied into each client.
avoid_when: The location is fixed, known at design time and never changes: a direct reference or constructor injection is simpler and checked by the compiler.
The resource is a compile-time dependency with exactly one implementation: static wiring beats a runtime registry addressed by strings.
The lookup would run on every use of a cheap, locally available object: resolve once at startup (eager acquisition) or inject it instead of looking it up per call.
The platform already resolves names for you (Kubernetes DNS plus a service mesh, the module system, the DI container) and you would only add a second indirection layer on top.
You cannot run a trustworthy lookup service (no authentication, no operating discipline for bindings): signed static configuration is safer than an unauthenticated registry.
anti_patterns: Lookup as a global service locator: every dependency is fetched by name from an ambient registry, so the dependency graph becomes invisible and tests must reproduce the whole registry.
Locations smuggled into names: binding values that embed host:port or file paths make the identifier unstable and the indirection fake - the name has to change whenever the resource moves.
Resolve once, never re-resolve: holding the first result forever (or a cache with no TTL or invalidation) turns every move of the resource into a stale-binding outage.
Unauthenticated registration: any component may bind or overwrite a name (or poison a cache), so resolution can be redirected to attacker-controlled resources.

Reinventing a lookup service over infrastructure that already provides one (a bespoke registry on top of DNS, the class loader or the DI container), adding a second source of truth for the same bindings.
design_principles: Indirection and location transparency: depend on the name, not on the address (program to an interface, resolve to a location).
Separation of concerns: resolution (finding the resource) is distinct from use (calling it) and from registration (publishing it).
Open/closed principle: new providers register bindings while the client side stays closed for modification.
Fail fast and tell the truth: an unresolvable name is an error, not a silent fallback to a guessed location, and 'not found' is a different failure from 'lookup unavailable'.
Single responsibility per role: the lookup service resolves, the registrar maintains bindings, the client uses the resource.
best_practices: Resolve through exactly one mediating service per name space; never let clients keep private fallback locations, or bindings diverge.
Choose the binding lifetime deliberately: TTLs, leases or change notifications; prefer short-lived leases with renewal over immortal bindings for anything that can move.
Keep names stable and location-free, version them only when the contract changes, and keep the name-to-resource mapping in one owned place.
Fail explicitly and distinguish 'name not found' from 'lookup service unavailable' - retry the latter with backoff and timeouts, never the former.
Authenticate and authorize both registration and resolution, treat the lookup service as a trust boundary, and log binding changes.

Use an existing standard infrastructure (DNS, JNDI, ServiceLoader, the DI container, entry points) before building a registry, and wrap it behind a typed client API rather than letting raw strings spread.
Scope names with a namespace or prefix hierarchy (e.g., 'prod/payments/v1', 'dev/auth') to prevent collisions and to allow environment-specific resolution from a single registry.

Instrument the lookup path: emit metrics on cache hit/miss ratios, lookup latency percentiles and binding age so stale TTLs and overloaded registry nodes surface in dashboards before they cause outages.
sources: Michael Kircher & Prashant Jain, Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management (Wiley, 2004) - Lookup (Resource Acquisition chapter, p. 21): find and access resources, local or distributed, through a mediating lookup service.

RFC 6762 (Multicast DNS): defines mDNS, a collaborative zero-configuration lookup protocol that resolves host names to IP addresses on a local link without a unicast DNS server. https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6762

RFC 6763 (DNS Service Discovery): defines DNS-SD, using DNS PTR and SRV record queries to discover named services available on the network, built on top of mDNS or unicast DNS. https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6763

HashiCorp Consul Documentation - Service Discovery and Health Checking: covers client-side service discovery, registered services with health checks, DNS and HTTP interfaces, and eventual consistency tradeoffs. https://developer.hashicorp.com/consul/docs/discovery/services

Kubernetes Services Documentation - DNS-based service discovery: describes how Kubernetes exposes Services as DNS names resolvable within the cluster, and how CoreDNS implements lookup for service-to-service communication.

Michael Kircher & Prashant Jain, "Lookup" (2001) - original pattern paper: defines Lookup as a service where providers register references and clients retrieve them through a location-transparent central point. http://www.kircher-schwanninger.de/michael/publications/Lookup.pdf

HashiCorp Consul Documentation - Discover services with Consul on Kubernetes: describes Consul DNS lookups, prepared queries, healthy instances and service failover. https://developer.hashicorp.com/consul/docs/discover/k8s

Kubernetes Documentation - DNS for Services and Pods: documents stable Service DNS names, namespace scoping, normal/headless A/AAAA records and SRV records. https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/dns-pod-service/

Mark Seemann, "Service Locator violates encapsulation": critique of ambient service locators hiding preconditions and causing runtime failures; informs the lookup misuse warning. https://blog.ploeh.dk/2015/10/26/service-locator-violates-encapsulation/

related_patterns_notes.cache-aside: Caches the result of a lookup by storing the resolved resource reference near the client, so repeated uses of the same name avoid a round-trip to the lookup service each time. TTL or lease policy on the cache entry must match the resource's mobility.
related_patterns_notes.caching: General pattern for storing previously looked-up values; lookup without caching incurs the full indirection cost on every call. A lookup service often serves as the backing store or the source of truth for a higher-level cache.
related_patterns_notes.eager-acquisition: Resolve and hold the resource at application startup, before it is first needed. Pairs well with lookup when the resource graph is known up-front and the cost of early resolution is acceptable; trades startup latency for per-call latency.
related_patterns_notes.lazy-acquisition: Defer the lookup to the point of first use. Natural companion to lookup: the resolve() call is the acquisition step. Works well when not all resources are needed on every run and startup time matters.
related_patterns_notes.partial-acquisition: Acquire only a subset of the resource's full representation (e.g., a stub or a reference) on first lookup, loading the rest on demand. The initial binding returned by the lookup service is the partial handle; subsequent method calls trigger full resolution.
related_patterns_notes.registry: The lookup service is a kind of registry: a shared, centrally-managed store of name-to-value bindings. The registry is the infrastructure that implements the lookup pattern; lookup is the client-facing behaviour the registry exposes.
related_patterns_notes.service-locator: A specific form of lookup where the locator itself is injected or accessed as a ambient global. Closely related but with a key distinction: the service locator pattern makes the locating mechanism a dependency that can be intercepted and mocked, whereas bare lookup delegates to an external service whose lifecycle is independent of the client.
